# collections

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/collections/

Data structures: vector and map, stack, queue, deque, set, linked list, priority queue and counter.

`Vector` and `HashMap`, which turn up in every program, are defined in this package, but you do not have to import it to use them. The rest, such as the stack and the queue, become available with `import collections`.

All of these are generic: you set the element type with `<...>`, as in `collections.Stack<str>`. All of them allocate, so write `defer ....free()` right after creating one.

Which should you pick? For an ordinary list, `Vector`; for "last in, first out", `Stack`; for "first in, first out", `Queue`; for adding and removing at both ends, `Deque`; for fast lookup by a key, `HashMap`; for removing duplicates, `Set`; and for "always give me the smallest", `PriorityQueue`.

## Types

### `LinkedList`

```salam
struct LinkedList<T>
```

A doubly linked list; adding and removing at either end is fast.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vals` | `Vector` | The values of the nodes. |
| `nxt` | `Vector` | The index of each node's next node. |
| `prv` | `Vector` | The index of each node's previous node. |
| `head` | `int` | The index of the first node. |
| `tail` | `int` | The index of the last node. |
| `freed` | `int` | The index of the first freed node, kept for reuse. |
| `count` | `int = 0` | The number of elements. |

collections-LinkedList.salam

```salam
import collections

func main:
    mut l := collections.LinkedList {} as collections.LinkedList<str>
    defer l.free()
    l.push_back("b")
    l.push_back("c")
    l.push_front("a")
    println l.to_vector(), l.size()
    println l.front_val(), l.back_val(), l.get(1)
    println l.pop_front(), l.pop_back(), l.size(), l.is_empty()
end
```

Output:

```text
["a", "b", "c"] 3
a c b
a c 1 false
```

```salam
import collections
import str

func main:
    mut c := collections.Counter {} as collections.Counter<str>
    defer c.free()
    each word in str.Fields("in the name of the friend"):
        c.add(word)
    end
    c.add_n("friend", 2)
    println c.count("the"), c.count("friend"), c.count("missing"), c.distinct()
end
```

### `PriorityQueue`

```salam
struct PriorityQueue<T>
```

A priority queue: the smallest element comes out each time, whatever order they went in. For scheduling work and for shortest path algorithms.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `h` | `Vector` | The elements as a binary heap. |

collections-PriorityQueue.salam

```salam
import collections

func main:
    mut q := collections.PriorityQueue {} as collections.PriorityQueue<int>
    defer q.free()
    each n in [5, 1, 4, 2, 3]:
        q.push(n)
    end
    println q.peek(), q.size()
    until not q.is_empty():
        print q.pop(), ""
    end
    println ""
end
```

Output:

```text
1 5
1 2 3 4 5
```

### `OrderedMap`

```salam
struct OrderedMap
```

A map from string to string that keeps the insertion order, for headers, settings and anywhere the display order matters.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `keys` | `Vector` | The keys in insertion order. |
| `vals` | `Vector` | The values in the same order. |
| `idx` | `HashMap` | A map from key to its position, for fast lookup. |

collections-OrderedMap.salam

```salam
import collections

func main:
    mut m := collections.OrderedMap {}
    defer m.free()
    m.set("name", "Salam")
    m.set("version", "0.5.0")
    m.set("language", "english")
    println m.len(), m.has("version"), m.get("name"), m.get_or("licence", "-")
    println m.index_of("language"), m.key_at(0), m.val_at(0)
    m.set_at(0, "Salam")
    println m.remove("version"), m.len()
    keys := m.clone_keys()
    println keys
end
```

Output:

```text
3 true Salam -
2 name Salam
1 2
["name", "language"]
```

### `Vector`

```salam
struct Vector<T>
```

A list whose size changes: the data structure you will use most. The elements sit next to each other in memory and access by index is immediate. You can also read and write elements with `[i]`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data` | `T*` | The address of the elements in memory. |

collections-Vector.salam

```salam
func main:
    mut v := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer v.free()
    v.reserve(8)
    println v.len(), v.cap() >= 8, v.is_empty()
    v.push(10)
    v.push(20)
    v.push(30)
    println v, v.first(), v.last(), v.get(1), v[2]
    v.set(0, 11)
    v[1] = 22
    v.insert(1, 15)
    println v
    println v.remove_at(1), v.pop(), v
    r := v.ref(0)
    r[0] = 99
    println v
    v.resize_set(v.len(), 7)
    println v
    v.clear()
    println v.len()
    mut z := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer z.free()
    z.zeros(3)
    println z
    mut a := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer a.free()
    a.alloc(4)
    println a.len()
end
```

Output:

```text
0 true true
[10, 20, 30] 10 30 20 30
[11, 15, 22, 30]
15 30 [11, 22]
[99, 22]
[99, 22, 7]
0
[0, 0, 0]
4
```

#### `reserve`

```salam
func reserve(need: int)
```

Reserves room for at least `need` elements in advance, so that later additions do not move the memory again.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: collections-Vector.salam

#### `ref`


Like `set`, but grows the vector when `i` is past the end. The slots between the old length and `i` have no defined value, so either fill them in order or start with `zeros`.

### `CircularList`

```salam
struct CircularList<T>
```

A circular list: after the last element you come back to the first, for taking turns in rotation, such as the players in a game.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `items` | `Vector` | The elements in the order they were added. |
| `head` | `int = 0` | The index of the current element. |

collections-CircularList.salam

```salam
import collections

func main:
    mut c := collections.CircularList {} as collections.CircularList<str>
    defer c.free()
    each name in ["Ali", "Sara", "Reza"]:
        c.add(name)
    end
    repeat 4:
        print c.current(), ""
        c.advance()
    end
    println ""
    c.rotate(1)
    println c.to_vector(), c.get(0), c.size(), c.is_empty()
end
```

Output:

```text
Ali Sara Reza Ali
["Reza", "Ali", "Sara"] Reza 3 false
```

### `HashMap`

```salam
struct HashMap<K, V>
```

A map from key to value with fast lookup, like a dictionary. The order of the entries is not predictable; if the insertion order matters, see `OrderedMap`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `keys` | `K*` | The address of the array of keys. |
| `vals` | `V*` | The address of the array of values. |
| `state` | `int*` | The state of each slot: empty, filled or removed. |
| `cap` | `int = 0` | The number of slots. |
| `count` | `int = 0` | The number of keys present. |
| `used` | `int = 0` | The number of slots in use, removed ones included. |

collections-HashMap.salam

```salam
func main:
    mut m := HashMap {} as HashMap<str, int>
    defer m.free()
    println m.is_empty()
    m.put("apple", 3)
    m.insert("pear", 5)
    m.put("apple", 4)
    println m.size(), m.has("apple"), m.get("apple"), m.get_or("banana", 0)
    println m.remove("pear"), m.remove("pear"), m.size()
    mut it := m.iter()
    until it.has_next():
        println it.key(), it.value()
        it.next()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
true
2 true 4 0
true false 1
apple 4
```

## Functions

### `contains`

```salam

```

True when `x` is in the vector.

collections-Funcs.salam

```salam
import collections

func main:
    mut a := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer a.free()
    each n in [1, 2, 3, 2, 5]:
        a.push(n)
    end
    println collections.contains(a, 3), collections.index_of(a, 2), collections.last_index_of(a, 2), collections.count_of(a, 2)
    println collections.reverse(a), collections.slice(a, 1, 3)
    b := collections.clone(a)
    collections.swap(a, 0, 4)
    println a, b
    mut c := Vector {} as Vector<int>
    defer c.free()
    collections.extend(c, b)
    collections.extend(c, b)
    println c.len()
end
```

Output:

```text
true 1 3 2
[5, 2, 3, 2, 1] [2, 3, 2]
[5, 2, 3, 2, 1] [1, 2, 3, 2, 5]
10
```

# os

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os/

Files, directories, system commands, program arguments and environment variables.

The `os` package is the simplest way to talk to the system: each function does one thing, and most of them take a file or directory path as a string. The functions that change something, such as `Remove` and `Mkdir`, return zero on success and some other number otherwise.

There are sub-packages for more specialised work: os.process for running other programs, os.shell for capturing command output, os.platform for identifying the system, and the fs.file and fs.dir packages, which do more.

## Types

### `FileInfo`

```salam
struct FileInfo
```

What `Stat` returns.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `i64 = 0` | The size of the file in bytes. |
| `is_dir` | `bool = false` | True when the path is a directory. |
| `exists` | `bool = false` | True when the path exists. |

os-Files.salam

```salam
import os

func main:
    os.WriteFile("note.txt", "first line\n")
    os.AppendFile("note.txt", "second line\n")
    print os.ReadFile("note.txt")
    println os.Exists("note.txt"), os.FileSize("note.txt")
    info := os.Stat("note.txt")
    println info.exists, info.is_dir, info.size
    os.Copy("note.txt", "copy.txt")
    os.Move("copy.txt", "new name.txt")
    println os.Exists("copy.txt"), os.Exists("new name.txt")
    os.Remove("new name.txt")
    println os.Exists("new name.txt")
    f := os.Open("note.txt", "rb")
    println f.readline()
    f.close()
end
```

Output:

```text
first line
second line
true 23
true false 23
false true
false
first line
```

### `CmdResult`

```salam
struct CmdResult
```

The result of running a command with `RunCapture`.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `int = 0` | The command's exit code; zero means success. |
| `out` | `str = ""` | The command's output. |

os-Run.salam

```salam
import os

func main:
    code := os.Run("echo from the shell")
    println "exit code:", code
    r := os.RunCapture("echo hello")
    println r.code, "[" + r.out + "]"
    println "[" + os.Output("echo world") + "]"
    println os.Pid() > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
from the shell
exit code: 0
0 [hello
]
[world
]
true
```

## Functions

### `Open`

```salam
func Open(path: str, mode: str): File*
```

Opens a file in the given mode: `"rb"` to read, `"wb"` to rewrite and `"ab"` to append. It returns null when it cannot.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-Files.salam

### `Exit`

```salam
func Exit(code: int)
```

Ends the program immediately with the given code. Inside `main` write `ret` instead, because exiting does not run the `defer` statements (error E109).

os-Args.salam

```salam
import os

func fail(message: str):
    printerrln message
    os.Exit(2)
end

func give_up():
    os.Abort()
end

func main:
    args := os.Args()
    println "argument count:", args.len()
    home := os.Env("HOME")
    println home.len() > 0 or os.Env("USERPROFILE").len() > 0
    if args.len() > 10:
        fail("too many arguments")
    end
    if args.len() > 100:
        give_up()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
argument count: 1
true
```

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-Args.salam

### `Mkdir`

```salam
func Mkdir(path: str): int
```

Creates a directory; the parent has to exist already.

os-Dirs.salam

```salam
import os

func main:
    os.Mkdir("project")
    os.MkdirAll("project/src/helpers")
    os.WriteFile("project/readme.txt", "hello")
    os.WriteFile("project/src/main.salam", "func main: end")
    println os.IsDir("project"), os.IsDir("project/readme.txt")
    println os.ListDir("project/src").len(), os.ListDirs("project")
    println os.Walk("project").len()
    os.CopyTree("project", "backup")
    println os.Exists("backup/src/main.salam")
    start := os.Cwd()
    os.Chdir("project")
    println os.Exists("readme.txt")
    os.Chdir(start)
    os.Rmdir("project/src/helpers")
    os.RemoveAll("project")
    os.RemoveAll("backup")
    println os.Exists("project"), os.TempDir().len() > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
2 ["src"]
2
true
true
false true
```

# os/error

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-error/

The last error from a file or process operation: its code, its message and the path that failed.

When an operation in the fs.file, fs.dir, os.process or `os.temp` packages fails, the detail is recorded here. After any operation that can fail, ask `HasError` and then `Last` to find out what happened.

The plain functions of the `os` package do not record errors here; they only return a code. This package is a different thing from the general-purpose error package.

## Types

### `OSError`

```salam
struct OSError
```

The detail of an error.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `int = 0` | The error code; one of the constants above. |
| `message` | `str = ""` | The error message, in English. |
| `operation` | `str = ""` | The name of the function that failed. |
| `path` | `str = ""` | The path that had the problem. |
| `system_code` | `int = 0` | The operating system's own error code (errno), where it is available. |

os-error-Last.salam

```salam
import os.error
import fs.file

func main:
    error.Clear()
    println error.HasError()
    file.Delete("a file that does not exist.txt")
    if error.HasError():
        e := error.Last()
        println e.code == error.FileNotFound, e.operation, e.message
        println error.LastCode(), error.LastMessage()
    end
    error.Set(error.Timeout, "time ran out", "waiting", "", 0)
    println error.LastCode() == error.Timeout, error.LastMessage()
    println error.None, error.PermissionDenied, error.AlreadyExists, error.InvalidPath, error.NotSupported, error.IOError, error.ProcessFailed
end
```

Output:

```text
false
true Delete delete failed
1 delete failed
true time ran out
0 2 3 4 5 6 8
```

## Constants and variables



```salam

```

It is already there.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-error-Last.salam

### `InvalidPath`

```salam
const InvalidPath: i32 = 4
```

The path is not valid.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-error-Last.salam

### `NotSupported`

```salam

```

This system does not support the operation.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-error-Last.salam

```salam

```

# os/process

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-process/

Running other programs, capturing their output, waiting for them and stopping them.

The `os.process` package runs another program directly, with no shell in between. The program's path and its arguments are given separately, so nothing has to be quoted and spaces or special characters in an argument cause no trouble.

If you need the program's output, run it with `StartCaptured`, wait for it to finish and then read the output. Call `Cleanup` when you are done.

## Types

### `Process`

```salam
struct Process
```

A process, running or finished.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pid` | `int = 0` | The process id. |
| `handle` | `void*` | The process handle on Windows. |
| `running` | `bool = false` | True while it is still running. |
| `exit_code` | `int = 0` | The exit code, once it has finished. |
| `stdout_path` | `str = ""` | The temporary file holding the captured output. |
| `stderr_path` | `str = ""` | The temporary file holding the captured error output. |

os-process-Start.salam

```salam
import os.process

func main:
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("hello from the child process")
    mut p := process.StartCaptured("/bin/echo", args)
    println process.Pid(p) > 0
    code := process.Wait(p)
    println code, process.ExitCode(p), process.IsRunning(p)
    print process.ReadStdout(p)
    println "[" + process.ReadStderr(p) + "]"
    process.Cleanup(p)
end
```

Output:

```text
true
0 0 false
hello from the child process
[]
```

## Functions

### `Start`

```salam
func Start(path: str, args: Vector<str>): Process
```

Runs a program with its arguments and does not wait; its output goes straight to your own program's output.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `StartCaptured`

```salam
func StartCaptured(path: str, args: Vector<str>): Process
```

Like `Start`, but captures the program's output and error output for you to read later.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `WaitPid`

```salam
func WaitPid(pid: int): int
```

Waits for the process with this id to finish and returns its exit code.

os-process-Kill.salam

```salam
import os.process

func main:
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("30")
    mut p := process.Start("/bin/sleep", args)
    println process.IsRunning(p)
    process.Terminate(p)
    process.Wait(p)
    println process.IsRunning(p)
    mut p2 := process.Start("/bin/sleep", args)
    process.Kill(p2)
    process.WaitPid(process.Pid(p2))
    println "both have stopped"
end
```

Output:

```text
true
false
both have stopped
```

### `Wait`

```salam
func Wait(p &: Process): int
```

Waits for the process to finish and returns its exit code.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `Fork`

```salam
func Fork(): int
```

Splits the current process in two: it returns zero in the child and the child's id in the parent. On Unix systems only; its example is not run here.

os-process-Fork.salam

```salam
import os.process

func main:
    pid := process.Fork()
    if pid == 0:
        println "I am the child"
        process.ExitNow(0)
    end
    process.WaitPid(pid)
    println "the child has finished"
end
```

### `ExitNow`

```salam

```

Ends the process immediately with no cleanup at all, for finishing a child after `Fork`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Fork.salam

### `Kill`

```salam

```

Kills the process at once (SIGKILL).

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Kill.salam

### `Terminate`

```salam
func Terminate(p &: Process): int
```

Asks the process to finish gracefully (SIGTERM) so it has a chance to clean up. On Windows it is the same as `Kill`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Kill.salam

### `ReadStdout`

```salam
func ReadStdout(p: Process): str
```

Reads the captured output once the process has finished.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `ReadStderr`

```salam
func ReadStderr(p: Process): str
```

Reads the captured error output.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `Cleanup`

```salam
func Cleanup(p &: Process)
```

Removes the temporary capture files.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `ExitCode`

```salam
func ExitCode(p: Process): int
```

The process's exit code.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

### `Pid`

```salam

```

The process id.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-process-Start.salam

# os/shell

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/os-shell/

Running a command and getting its exit code, its output and its errors together.

The `os.shell` package runs a command and gives back the whole result at once: the exit code, the output and the error output.

`Exec` splits the command on spaces alone and no shell is involved: pipes (`|`), redirection (`>`) and quoting do not work. For those, call `sh -c` through `Run`, as the example does.

## Types

### `CmdResult`

```salam
struct CmdResult
```

The result of a command.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `int = 0` | The exit code; zero means success. |
| `out` | `str = ""` | The standard output. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The error output. |

os-shell-Run.salam

```salam
import os.shell

func main:
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("-n")
    args.push("hello")
    r := shell.Run("echo", args)
    println r.code, "[" + r.out + "]"
    r2 := shell.Exec("echo one two three")
    println r2.code, "[" + r2.out + "]"
    mut args2 := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args2.free()
    args2.push("-c")
    args2.push("echo oops >&2; exit 3")
    r3 := shell.Run("sh", args2)
    println r3.code, "[" + r3.err + "]"
    println shell.System("true"), shell.System("false") != 0
end
```

Output:

```text
0 [hello]
0 [one two three
]
3 [oops
]
0 true
```

## Functions

### `Run`

```salam
func Run(command: str, args: Vector<str>): CmdResult
```

Runs a program with its arguments given separately and waits for it to finish.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

### `Exec`

```salam
func Exec(command: str): CmdResult
```

Splits a command string on spaces into a program and its arguments and runs it, with no shell.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

### `System`

```salam
func System(command: str): int
```

Runs a command in the real shell (`/bin/sh` or `cmd`) and returns only the exit code; the output is printed directly.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: os-shell-Run.salam

# fs

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs/

File times and permissions; the base of the file, dir and path packages.

The `fs` package holds a few shared functions and three sub-packages you will use far more often: fs.file, fs.dir and fs.path. Times are in seconds since the start of 1970, Unix time.

Write permissions in octal, such as `0o644`, meaning the owner reads and writes and everyone else reads. `Permissions` returns the same digits as an ordinary number, such as `644`, so that it reads easily.

## Functions

### `ModTime`

```salam
func ModTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file's content was last changed.

fs-ModTime.salam

```salam
import fs
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("report.txt", "hello")
    t := fs.ModTime("report.txt")
    println t > 0, fs.AccessedTime("report.txt") > 0, fs.CreatedTime("report.txt") >= 0
    fs.Chmod("report.txt", 0o644)
    println fs.Permissions("report.txt")
end
```

Output:

```text
true true true
644
```

### `AccessedTime`

```salam
func AccessedTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file was last read.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `CreatedTime`

```salam
func CreatedTime(path: str): i64
```

When the file was created, or zero where the system does not keep it.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `Chmod`

```salam
func Chmod(path: str, mode: int): int
```

Changes a file's permissions; give them in octal, such as `0o644`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

### `Permissions`

```salam
func Permissions(path: str): int
```

A file's permissions, as octal digits, such as `644`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-ModTime.salam

# fs/dir

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-dir/

Creating, listing, copying, moving and removing directories.

The `fs.dir` package covers everything you do with directories. When a function fails it records the detail in the os.error package.

Note that `Exists` here is true only for a directory; for files use `fs.file.Exists`.

## Functions

### `Mkdir`

```salam
func Mkdir(p: str): int
```

Creates one directory.

fs-dir-List.salam

```salam
import fs.dir
import fs.file

func main:
    dir.Mkdir("library")
    dir.MkdirAll("library/poetry/hafez")
    file.WriteText("library/index.txt", "3 books")
    file.WriteText("library/poetry/hafez/ghazal.txt", "a line of verse")
    println dir.Exists("library"), dir.IsDir("library/index.txt")
    println dir.List("library").len(), dir.ListDirs("library"), dir.ListFiles("library")
    println dir.Walk("library").len(), dir.Size("library") > 0
    println dir.Permissions("library") > 0, dir.ModTime("library") > 0
    dir.Copy("library", "backup")
    dir.Move("backup", "archive")
    println dir.Exists("backup"), dir.Exists("archive/poetry/hafez"), file.Exists("archive/poetry/hafez/ghazal.txt")
    dir.Mkdir("empty")
    dir.Remove("empty")
    dir.RemoveAll("library")
    dir.RemoveAll("archive")
    println dir.Exists("library"), dir.Exists("empty")
end
```

Output:

```text
true false
2 ["poetry"] ["index.txt"]
2 true
true true
false true true
false false
```

### `MkdirAll`

```salam
func MkdirAll(p: str): int
```

Creates a directory along with every parent it needs.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-dir-List.salam

# fs/file

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-file/

Reading and writing files, file information, copying and moving, and MD5 and SHA digests.

The `fs.file` package is the fullest set of tools for working with files. For settings and anything else that matters, use `AtomicWrite`: it writes to a temporary file and then replaces the original, so an interrupted program never leaves a half written file behind.

## Types

### `FileInfo`

```salam
struct FileInfo
```

Everything about a file.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `i64 = 0` | The size in bytes. |
| `mod_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was last changed. |
| `accessed_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was last read. |
| `created_time` | `i64 = 0` | When it was created. |
| `permissions` | `int = 0` | The permissions, as octal digits. |
| `exists` | `bool = false` | True when the file exists. |

fs-file-Stat.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("picture.png", "PNG")
    info := file.Stat("picture.png")
    println info.exists, info.size, info.mod_time > 0, info.permissions > 0
    println file.Size("picture.png"), file.Exists("picture.png")
    println file.ModTime("picture.png") > 0, file.AccessedTime("picture.png") > 0, file.CreatedTime("picture.png") >= 0
    file.Chmod("picture.png", 0o600)
    println file.Permissions("picture.png")
    println file.Extension("picture.png"), file.MimeType("picture.png"), file.MimeType("letter.pdf")
    println file.Stat("missing.txt").exists
end
```

Output:

```text
true 3 true true
3 true
true true true
600
.png image/png application/pdf
false
```

## Functions

### `Open`

```salam
func Open(path: str, mode: str): File*
```

Opens a file to work through it piece by piece; the modes are the same as os.Open.

fs-file-ReadText.salam

```salam
import fs.file

func main:
    file.WriteText("poem.txt", "The children of Adam are limbs of one body\n")
    file.Append("poem.txt", "having been created of one essence\n")
    print file.ReadText("poem.txt")
    println file.ReadAll("poem.txt") == file.ReadText("poem.txt")
    lines := file.ReadLines("poem.txt")
    println lines.len(), lines.get(1)
    file.WriteBytes("data.bin", "ABCDEF")
    println file.ReadBytes("data.bin", 3)
    file.AtomicWrite("settings.txt", "language=english")
    println file.ReadText("settings.txt")
    f := file.Open("poem.txt", "rb")
    println f.readline()
    file.Close(f)
end
```

Output:

```text
The children of Adam are limbs of one body
having been created of one essence
true
2 having been created of one essence
ABC
language=english
The children of Adam are limbs of one body
```

# fs/path

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/fs-path/

Working with file paths: joining them, separating the name and the extension, absolute and relative paths, and a safety check.

Do not build paths by concatenating strings; `Join` puts the right separator in for you. When a path comes from a user, check it with `IsSafe` before opening it, so that nobody climbs out of the permitted directory with `../..`.

## Types

### `PathParts`

```salam
struct PathParts
```

The two parts of a path.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dir` | `str = ""` | The directory part. |
| `base` | `str = ""` | The file name. |

fs-path-Join.salam

```salam
import fs.path

func main:
    p := path.Join("/home/sara", "docs/cv.pdf")
    println p
    parts := path.Split(p)
    println parts.dir, parts.base
    println path.Dirname(p), path.Parent(p), path.Filename(p), path.Basename(p)
    println path.Ext(p), path.Stem(p)
    println path.Normalize("/a/./b/../c//d"), path.Clean("a/b/../../c")
    println path.IsAbs(p), path.IsAbs("docs"), path.IsAbs(path.Abs("docs"))
    println path.Rel("/home/sara", "/home/sara/docs/cv.pdf")
    println path.IsSafe("/srv/files", "a/b.txt"), path.IsSafe("/srv/files", "../../etc/passwd")
    println path.Validate("docs/cv.pdf"), path.Validate("")
end
```

Output:

```text
/home/sara/docs/cv.pdf
/home/sara/docs cv.pdf
/home/sara/docs /home/sara/docs cv.pdf cv
.pdf cv
/a/./b/../c//d c
true false true
docs/cv.pdf
true false
true false
```

## Functions

```salam

```

Turns Windows `\` separators into `/` and does nothing else. To resolve `..` and `.`, see `Clean`.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-path-Join.salam

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: fs-path-Join.salam

True when the path is absolute.

# filepath

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/filepath/

Path functions that never touch the file system; the same work as the fs/path package.

The `filepath` package works on strings alone and never touches the file system, apart from `Abs`, which needs the current directory. The fs.path package is built on it; use whichever reads better to you.

## Constants and variables

### `Separator`

```salam
const Separator: str = "/"
```

The separator between the parts of a path: `/`.

filepath-Join.salam

```salam
import filepath

func main:
    p := filepath.Join("projects", "salam/main.salam")
    println p, filepath.Separator
    println filepath.Dir(p), filepath.Base(p), filepath.Ext(p), filepath.Stem(p)
    println filepath.Normalize("a//b/./c/"), filepath.Clean("a/b/../c")
    println filepath.IsAbs("/usr/bin"), filepath.IsAbs(p), filepath.IsAbs(filepath.Abs(p))
    println filepath.Rel("/a/b", "/a/b/c/d")
    println filepath.IsSafe("/srv", "x/y"), filepath.IsSafe("/srv", "../etc")
    println filepath.Validate("a/b")
end
```

Output:

```text
projects/salam/main.salam /
projects/salam main.salam .salam main
a//b/./c/ a/c
true false true
c/d
true false
true
```

# env

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/env/

Environment variables: reading them with the right type, .env files, the run profile, and masking sensitive values.

Settings such as a server port, a database address and API keys belong in environment variables rather than in the code. The `env` package reads them with the right type and gives you a default when they are not set. It can load them from a `.env` file too.

The "profile" is read from `SALAM_ENV` and says whether the program is running in development, test or production.

## Functions

### `Get`

```salam
func Get(name: str): str
```

The value of a variable, or an empty string.

env-Get.salam

```salam
import env

func main:
    env.Set("PORT", "8080")
    env.Set("DEBUG", "true")
    env.Set("RATIO", "0.75")
    println env.Get("PORT"), env.Has("PORT"), env.Has("NOPE")
    println env.GetInt("PORT", 80), env.GetInt("NOPE", 80)
    println env.GetBool("DEBUG", false), env.GetFloat("RATIO", 1.0)
    println env.GetOr("HOST", "localhost")
    env.Unset("PORT")
    println env.Has("PORT")
    env.Set("API_KEY", "example-not-a-real-key")
    println env.Mask("example-not-a-real-key"), env.GetMasked("API_KEY")
    env.Set("NAME", "Salam")
    println env.Expand("${NAME} on port ${PORT:-3000}")
end
```

Output:

```text
8080 true false
8080 80
true 0.75
localhost
false
ex****ey ex****ey
Salam on port 3000
```

### `Load`

```salam
func Load(path: str): int
```

Loads a `KEY=VALUE` file without changing variables that are already set. It returns how many variables were read.

env-Load.salam

```salam
import env
import io

func main:
    io.WriteFile(".env", "DB_HOST=localhost\nDB_PORT=5432\n# a comment\n")
    println env.Load(".env"), env.Get("DB_HOST")
    env.Set("DB_PORT", "1")
    env.Load(".env")
    println env.Get("DB_PORT")
    env.Overload(".env")
    println env.Get("DB_PORT")
    println env.LoadText("A=1\nB=2"), env.Get("B")
    println env.LoadDotEnv(".env")
    io.WriteFile(".env.test", "MODE=testing\n")
    env.Set("SALAM_ENV", "test")
    println env.LoadProfile("."), env.Get("MODE")
end
```

Output:

```text
2 localhost
1
5432
2 2
2
1 testing
```

### `Overload`

```salam
func Overload(path: str): int
```

Like `Load`, but it replaces existing variables with the file's values too.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: env-Load.salam

### `LoadText`


# flag

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/flag/

Reading command line options such as `--port 8080` and `-v` with the right type, and generating the help text.

The `flag` package reads command line options. Each flag has a long name (`--port`), a short name (`-p`), a default value and a line of help. The value can be given either way: `--port=8080` or `--port 8080`. Any argument that is not a flag is "positional", and after `--` everything counts as positional.

`--help` and `-h` are always recognised and the `Usage` text is generated for you. Pass `Parse` the arguments without the program's own name.

## Types

### `FlagSet`

```salam
struct FlagSet
```

A program's set of flags and the result of parsing.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prog` | `str = ""` | The program's name, for the help text. |
| `desc` | `str = ""` | The program's description, for the help text. |
| `names` | `Vector` | The long names of the flags. |
| `shorts` | `Vector` | The short names of the flags. |
| `kinds` | `Vector` | The kind of each flag. |
| `vals` | `Vector` | The current value of each flag, as text. |
| `defs` | `Vector` | The default value of each flag. |
| `helps` | `Vector` | The help line of each flag. |
| `was_set` | `Vector` | Whether each flag appeared on the command line. |
| `pos` | `Vector` | The positional arguments. |
| `err` | `str = ""` | The message of the last parse error. |
| `help_wanted` | `bool = false` | True when `--help` was given. |

flag-Parse.salam

```salam
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("copy", "copies files")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "verbose", "v", false, "report everything")
    flag.AddStr(f, "out", "o", "output", "the destination directory")
    flag.AddInt(f, "jobs", "j", 1, "how many jobs at once")
    flag.AddFloat(f, "ratio", "r", 1.0, "the compression ratio")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    each a in ["-v", "--out=backup", "-j", "4", "a.txt", "b.txt"]:
        args.push(a)
    end
    println flag.Parse(f, args), "[" + flag.Error(f) + "]"
    println flag.GetBool(f, "verbose"), flag.GetStr(f, "out"), flag.GetInt(f, "jobs"), flag.GetFloat(f, "ratio")
    println flag.WasSet(f, "jobs"), flag.WasSet(f, "ratio")
    println flag.Positional(f), flag.HelpWanted(f)
    println flag.FlagKindBool, flag.FlagKindStr, flag.FlagKindInt, flag.FlagKindFloat
end
```

Output:

```text
true []
true backup 4 1
true false
["a.txt", "b.txt"] false
0 1 2 3
```

```salam
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("tool", "an example tool")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddBool(f, "quiet", "q", false, "say nothing")
    flag.AddInt(f, "port", "p", 8080, "the port")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("--help")
    flag.Parse(f, args)
    if flag.HelpWanted(f):
        print flag.Usage(f)
    end
    mut bad := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer bad.free()
    bad.push("--port=abc")
    mut f2 := flag.New("tool", "")
    defer flag.Free(f2)
    flag.AddInt(f2, "port", "p", 8080, "the port")
    println flag.Parse(f2, bad), flag.Error(f2)
end
```

Output:

```text

  an example tool
Options:
  -q, --quiet  say nothing
  -p, --port <int>  the port (default: 8080)
  -h, --help  show this help
false invalid int value for --port: abc
```

# cli

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/cli/

Command line programs with several commands, like `git commit`, and asking the user questions.

Many tools have several commands: `salam build`, `salam run`. The `cli` package registers the commands, works out from the first argument which one was asked for, and builds the overall help text. For each command's own flags, use the flag package alongside it.

`Prompt` and `Confirm` ask the user something in the terminal; their example is not run here because it would wait for an answer.

## Types

### `App`

```salam
struct App
```

A command line program and its commands.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `str = ""` | The program's name. |
| `desc` | `str = ""` | The program's description. |
| `version` | `str = ""` | The program's version. |
| `cmd_names` | `Vector` | The names of the commands. |
| `cmd_descs` | `Vector` | The descriptions of the commands. |

cli-Dispatch.salam

```salam
import cli
import str

func run(app &: cli.App, line: str):
    args := str.Split(line, " ")
    command := cli.Dispatch(app, args)
    if command == cli.CmdHelp:
        println "help was asked for"
    else command == cli.CmdVersion:
        println "version:", app.version
    else command == cli.CmdUnknown:
        println "unknown command"
    else:
        println "running:", command, cli.RemainingArgs(args)
    end
    args.free()
end

func main:
    mut app := cli.New("salamctl", "project management", "1.0.0")
    cli.Register(app, "build", "build the project")
    cli.Register(app, "test", "run the tests")
    println cli.HasCommand(app, "build"), cli.CommandDesc(app, "test")
    each line in ["build --fast", "--help", "--version", "deploy"]:
        run(app, line)
    end
    print cli.Usage(app)
end
```

Output:

```text
true run the tests
running: build ["--fast"]
help was asked for
version: 1.0.0
unknown command
salamctl 1.0.0
project management

Usage: salamctl <command> [options]

Commands:
  build         build the project
  test          run the tests

Run 'salamctl <command> --help' for help on a specific command.
```

## Constants and variables

### `CmdHelp`

```salam
const CmdHelp: str = "__help__"
```

What `Dispatch` returns when help was asked for, or no argument was given.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: cli-Dispatch.salam

### `CmdVersion`

```salam
const CmdVersion: str = "__version__"
```

What `Dispatch` returns when the version was asked for.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: cli-Dispatch.salam

### `CmdUnknown`

```salam
const CmdUnknown: str = "__unknown__"
```

What `Dispatch` returns for a command that was never registered.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: cli-Dispatch.salam

## Functions

### `New`

```salam

```

Creates a program with a name, a description and a version.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: cli-Dispatch.salam

```salam

```

```salam

```

The description of a command.


### `RequireFlags`

```salam

```

Of the names you give, returns the flags that did not appear on the command line; for required flags.

cli-RequireFlags.salam

```salam
import cli
import flag

func main:
    mut f := flag.New("deploy", "")
    defer flag.Free(f)
    flag.AddStr(f, "host", "h", "", "the server")
    flag.AddStr(f, "user", "u", "", "the user")
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("--host=example.com")
    flag.Parse(f, args)
    mut required := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer required.free()
    required.push("host")
    required.push("user")
    println "missing:", cli.RequireFlags(f, required)
end
```

Output:

```text
missing: ["user"]
```

# config

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/config/

Reading and writing INI, env and YAML settings files with dotted keys.

The `config` package keeps settings as an ordered list of keys and values. Keys in sections are dotted: the key `host` in the `[db]` section of an INI file, or under `db:` in YAML, becomes `db.host`.

The usual pattern is to read the default settings, `Merge` the current environment's settings on top, and then read the values with the right type.

## Types

### `Config`

```salam
struct Config
```

A set of settings.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `m` | `collections.OrderedMap` | The ordered map that keeps the keys and values in order. |

config-Get.salam

```salam
import config

func main:
    mut c := config.New()
    defer config.Free(c)
    config.Set(c, "name", "salam")
    config.Set(c, "port", "8080")
    config.Set(c, "debug", "yes")
    config.Set(c, "ratio", "0.5")
    println config.Len(c), config.Has(c, "port"), config.Get(c, "name")
    println config.GetInt(c, "port", 80), config.GetFloat(c, "ratio", 1.0), config.GetBool(c, "debug", false)
    println config.GetOr(c, "host", "localhost")
    println config.Remove(c, "ratio"), config.Keys(c)
end
```

Output:

```text
4 true salam
8080 0.5 true
localhost
true ["name", "port", "debug"]
```

config-ParseINI.salam

```salam
import config
import io

func main:
    text := "name = salam\n\n[db]\nhost = localhost\nport = 5432\n"
    mut c := config.ParseINI(text)
    defer config.Free(c)
    println config.Keys(c)
    mut db := config.Section(c, "db")
    defer config.Free(db)
    println config.Get(db, "port")
    print config.FormatINI(db)
    io.WriteFile("app.ini", text)
    mut loaded := config.LoadINI("app.ini")
    defer config.Free(loaded)
    println config.Get(loaded, "db.host")
end
```

Output:

```text
["name", "db.host", "db.port"]
5432
host = localhost
port = 5432
localhost
```


```salam
import config
import io

func main:
    mut base := config.ParseEnv("MODE=dev\nPORT=3000\n")
    mut over := config.ParseEnv("PORT=80\nLOG=info\n")
    defer config.Free(base)
    defer config.Free(over)
    mut merged := config.Merge(base, over)
    defer config.Free(merged)
    print config.FormatEnv(merged)
    print config.FormatEnvExport(over)
    io.WriteFile(".env", "TOKEN=abc\n")
    mut loaded := config.LoadEnv(".env")
    defer config.Free(loaded)
    println config.Get(loaded, "TOKEN")
end
```

Output:

```text

PORT=80
LOG=info
export PORT=80
export LOG=info
abc
```

# log

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/log/

Recording what a program does, with levels, a prefix, structured fields, JSON output and writing to a file.

For a program running on a server, `println` is not enough: you need to know how important each message is and when it was written, and to be able to silence the unimportant ones. The `log` package has four levels, debug, info, warn and error, and records only the messages at or above the level you set; the default level is info.

By default the log goes to standard error with a timestamp. The examples below turn the time off so their output is stable.

## Constants and variables

### `LevelDebug`

```salam
const LevelDebug: i32 = 0
```

The debug level: detail for whoever is working on the code.

log-Info.salam

```salam
import log

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    log.SetPrefix("[app]")
    log.Debug("this is not shown")
    log.Info("the server is ready")
    log.Warn("memory is running low")
    log.Error("the connection dropped")
    log.SetLevel(log.LevelDebug)
    log.Debug("now it is shown")
    log.Log(log.LevelWarn, "at a level of my choosing")
    println log.GetLevel(), log.LevelName(log.LevelError), log.ParseLevel("warn"), log.LevelInfo
end
```

Output:

```text
[INFO] [app] the server is ready
[WARN] [app] memory is running low
[ERROR] [app] the connection dropped
[DEBUG] [app] now it is shown
[WARN] [app] at a level of my choosing
0 ERROR 2 1
```

### `LevelInfo`

```salam
const LevelInfo: i32 = 1
```

The info level: ordinary events.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: log-Info.salam

### `LevelWarn`

```salam
const LevelWarn: i32 = 2
```

The warn level: something unusual, but not an error.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: log-Info.salam

### `LevelError`

```salam
const LevelError: i32 = 3
```

The error level.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: log-Info.salam

### `FormatText`

```salam
const FormatText: i32 = 0
```

The readable text format.

log-InfoKV.salam

```salam
import log

func main:
    log.ToStdout()
    log.ShowTime(false)
    mut keys := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    mut values := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer keys.free()
    defer values.free()
    keys.push("user")
    values.push("sara")
    keys.push("ms")
    values.push("42")
    log.InfoKV("request served", keys, values)
    log.WarnKV("it was slow", keys, values)
    log.ErrorKV("it failed", keys, values)
    log.SetLevel(log.LevelDebug)
    log.DebugKV("the details", keys, values)
    log.SetFormat(log.FormatJSON)
    log.Info("as JSON")
    println log.GetFormat() == log.FormatJSON, log.FormatText
    mut fields := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer fields.free()
    fields.push(log.Field("path", "/login"))
    fields.push(log.FieldInt("status", 200))
    fields.push(log.FieldBool("cached", false))
    println log.KV("response", fields)
end
```

Output:

```text
[INFO] request served user=sara ms=42
[WARN] it was slow user=sara ms=42
[ERROR] it failed user=sara ms=42
[DEBUG] the details user=sara ms=42
{"level": "INFO", "msg": "as JSON"}
true 0
response path=/login status=200 cached=false
```

# debug

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/debug/

Tools for finding a bug: assertions, a hand-kept call stack, tracing and timing.

The `debug` package holds a few simple tools for when the program is not doing the right thing. `Assert` checks a condition that should always hold. `Enter` and `Exit` build a call stack by hand, so you know where in the program you are. The timers show which part is slow.

## Functions

### `Assert`

```salam
func Assert(cond: bool, msg: str)
```

If the condition is false, prints the message and stops the program.

debug-Enter.salam

```salam
import debug

func child():
    debug.Enter("child")
    println debug.Depth()
    println debug.Stack()
    debug.Exit()
end

func main:
    debug.Enter("root")
    child()
    debug.Exit()
    println debug.Depth()
    debug.Assert(1 + 1 == 2, "the arithmetic holds")
    debug.AssertNotNil(debug.MemStats() as void*, "the memory statistics")
    debug.EnableTrace(true)
    println debug.TraceEnabled()
    debug.Trace("a trace message")
    debug.StartTimer("loop")
    mut total := 0
    repeat 1000 in i:
        total += i
    end
    println total, debug.StopTimer("loop") >= 0.0
    if total < 0:
        debug.Break()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
2
root > child
0
true
[TRACE] a trace message
499500 true
```

### `AssertNotNil`

```salam

```

If the pointer is null, stops with the message.

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: debug-Enter.salam

Adds a step's name to the hand-kept stack, usually at the start of a function.

# runtime

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/runtime/

Facts about the running program: the system, the memory, the uptime and the build options.

The `runtime` package is useful for reporting a program's state, on a `/health` route on a server for instance. The uptime is counted from the moment `MarkStart` was called.

Free and used memory are available on Linux and Windows only; on other systems those functions return minus one.

## Functions

### `OS`

```salam
func OS(): str
```

The name of the operating system.

runtime-Summary.salam

```salam
import runtime

func main:
    runtime.MarkStart()
    println runtime.OS().len() > 0, runtime.Arch().len() > 0, runtime.CpuCount() >= 1
    free := runtime.AvailableMemory()
    used := runtime.UsedMemory()
    println runtime.TotalMemory() > 0, free > 0 or free == -1, used >= 0 or used == -1
    println runtime.UptimeMs() >= 0, runtime.UptimeSeconds() >= 0.0
    println runtime.IsAsanBuild(), runtime.IsMemDebugBuild()
    println runtime.IsSafeBuild() or not runtime.IsSafeBuild()
    println runtime.BuildFlags().len() >= 0, runtime.Summary().len() > 0
end
```

Output:

```text
true true true
true true true
true true
false false
true
true true
```

# testing

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/testing/

Writing tests for your code: equality assertions, a pass and fail count, and a summary at the end.

A test is a small program that checks your code does what it should. The `testing` package has assertions that print a clear message when they fail but do not stop the program, so every test runs and `Summary` says at the end how many passed and how many failed.

The value `Summary` returns is the number of failures. Return it from `main` so that the test program ends with a non-zero code in CI.

## Functions

### `Assert`

```salam
func Assert(cond: bool)
```

Records a failure when the condition is false.

testing-Assert.salam

```salam
import testing

func add(a: int, b: int): int:
    ret a + b
end

func main:
    testing.Reset()
    testing.Assert(add(2, 2) == 4)
    testing.AssertMsg(add(1, 1) == 2, "one and one")
    testing.AssertTrue(true)
    testing.AssertFalse(add(0, 0) == 1)
    testing.AssertEqInt(add(3, 4), 7)
    testing.AssertEqInt64(10000000000 as i64, 10000000000 as i64)
    testing.AssertEqFloat(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, 0.0001)
    testing.AssertContains("the Salam language", "Salam")
    testing.AssertEqStr("hello", "hello")
    testing.AssertEqBool(1 < 2, true)
    testing.AssertNeInt(1, 2)
    testing.AssertNeStr("a", "b")
    testing.AssertNil(null)
    testing.AssertEqInt(add(2, 2), 5)
    println testing.Passed(), testing.Failed()
    println testing.Summary()
end
```

Output:

```text
FAIL: ints differ: got 4 want 5
13 1
--
tests: 13 passed, 1 failed
1
```

# error

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/error/

Structured errors with a kind, a message, a chain of causes, metadata and a retry policy.

A function that may fail can return an `error.Error`: either "nil", meaning everything went well, or an error with a kind, such as "not found", and a message. The kind is for the code to decide on; the message is for a person to read.

When an error comes up from a lower layer, `Wrap` it so the current layer's explanation is added. The final message shows the whole chain, as in "could not save the report: the disk is full", and `RootMessage` gives the original cause.

For transient errors, such as a dropped network connection, `RetryPolicy` says when and how often to try again and how long to wait between attempts; the delay doubles each time.

## Types

### `Error`

```salam
struct Error
```

An error.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind` | `str = ""` | The kind of the error: one of the constants above, or one you define yourself. |
| `messages` | `Vector` | The message from each layer, from the innermost cause to the outermost. |
| `kinds` | `Vector` | The kind of each layer. |
| `trace` | `Vector` | The places the error has passed through. |
| `meta_keys` | `Vector` | The metadata keys. |
| `meta_vals` | `Vector` | The metadata values. |

error-New.salam

```salam
import error

func find_user(id: int): error.Error:
    if id <= 0:
        ret error.New(error.KindInvalidArgument, "the id has to be positive")
    end
    if id > 100:
        ret error.NewAt(error.KindNotFound, "no such user", "find_user")
    end
    ret error.Nil()
end

func main:
    each id in [7, -1, 500]:
        mut e := find_user(id)
        if error.Ok(e):
            println id, "found", error.IsNil(e)
        else:
            println id, error.Kind(e), error.Message(e)
            println error.Is(e, error.KindNotFound), error.IsNotFound(e), error.IsInvalidArgument(e)
        end
        error.Free(e)
    end
    mut args := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    defer args.free()
    args.push("config.ini")
    e2 := error.Newf(error.KindIO, "cannot read {}", args)
    println error.Message(e2)
end
```

Output:

```text
7 found true
-1 invalid_argument the id has to be positive
false false true
500 not_found no such user
true true false
cannot read config.ini
```

### `RetryPolicy`

```salam
struct RetryPolicy
```

A retry policy.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_attempts` | `int = 3` | The greatest number of attempts; three by default. |
| `base_delay_ms` | `int = 100` | The delay after the first failed attempt, in milliseconds; 100 by default. |
| `max_delay_ms` | `int = 5000` | The ceiling on the delay, in milliseconds; 5000 by default. |

error-RetryPolicy.salam

```salam
import error

func main:
    mut policy := error.NewRetryPolicy(4, 100, 1000)
    println policy.max_attempts, policy.base_delay_ms, policy.max_delay_ms
    e := error.New(error.KindTimeout, "the server did not answer")
    mut attempt := 1
    until error.ShouldRetry(policy, e, attempt):
        println "attempt", attempt, "after", error.DelayForAttempt(policy, attempt), "milliseconds"
        attempt += 1
    end
    println error.ShouldRetry(policy, error.New(error.KindInvalidArgument, "bad input"), 1)
end
```

Output:

```text
4 100 1000
attempt 1 after 100 milliseconds
attempt 2 after 200 milliseconds
attempt 3 after 400 milliseconds
false
```

error-Wrap.salam

```salam
import error

func main:
    root := error.New(error.KindIO, "the disk is full")
    a := error.Wrap(root, "could not save the report")
    b := error.WrapAt(a, "the nightly run stopped", "nightly job")
    c := error.WrapKind(b, error.KindInternal, "internal error")
    d := error.WithMeta(c, "disk", "/dev/sda1")
    println error.Message(d)
    println error.RootMessage(d)
    println error.Kind(d), error.IsInternal(d), error.Meta(d, "disk")
    println error.Trace(d)
    println error.Format(d)
end
```

Output:

```text
internal error: the nightly run stopped: could not save the report: the disk is full
the disk is full
internal true /dev/sda1
nightly job
[internal] internal error: the nightly run stopped: could not save the report: the disk is full
  trace: nightly job
  disk=/dev/sda1
```

# mem

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/mem/

Working with memory directly: allocating and freeing, copying, arenas and pools, and leak checking.

Most programs never need this package: vectors, maps and strings look after their own memory. The `mem` package is for low-level work, such as talking to a C library or building a data structure of your own. Everything you take with `Allocate` has to be given back with `Free`.

An arena is one large block you take pieces off the front of and then release all at once; it is very fast for work with many small objects that share a lifetime. A pool hands out and takes back blocks of one fixed size.

## Types

### `Arena`

```salam
struct Arena
```

A memory arena.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `buf` | `void*` | The address of the arena's memory. |
| `cap` | `u64 = 0` | The capacity in bytes. |
| `used` | `u64 = 0` | How much has been taken. |

mem-Arena.salam

```salam
import mem

func main:
    mut arena := mem.NewArena(1024 as u64)
    println mem.ArenaCapacity(arena), mem.ArenaUsed(arena)
    a := mem.ArenaAlloc(arena, 100 as u64)
    b := mem.ArenaAllocZeroed(arena, 200 as u64)
    println a != null, b != null, mem.ArenaUsed(arena) >= 300, mem.ArenaRemaining(arena) <= 724
    println mem.ArenaAlloc(arena, 4000 as u64) == null
    mem.ArenaReset(arena)
    println mem.ArenaUsed(arena), arena.cap
    mem.ArenaFree(arena)
end
```

Output:

```text
1024 0
true true true true
true
0 1024
```

### `Pool`

```salam
struct Pool
```

A pool of equally sized blocks.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `block_size` | `u64 = 0` | The size of each block. |
| `block_count` | `u64 = 0` | The number of blocks. |
| `blocks` | `void*` | The address of the blocks' memory. |
| `free_list` | `void*` | The list of free blocks. |

mem-Pool.salam

```salam
import mem

func main:
    mut pool := mem.NewPool(32 as u64, 4 as u64)
    println mem.PoolBlockSize(pool), mem.PoolCapacity(pool)
    b1 := mem.PoolAlloc(pool)
    b2 := mem.PoolAlloc(pool)
    println b1 != null, b2 != null, b1 != b2
    mem.PoolFree(pool, b1)
    b3 := mem.PoolAlloc(pool)
    println b3 == b1
    mem.PoolDestroy(pool)
end
```

Output:

```text
32 4
true true true
true
```

### `Allocate`

```salam
func Allocate(size: u64): void*
```

Takes a piece of memory of the given size; its contents are undefined.

mem-Allocate.salam

```salam
import mem

func main:
    b := mem.Allocate(8 as u64)
    mem.Set(b, 0, 8 as u64)
    bytes := b as i8*
    bytes[0] = 65 as i8
    bytes[1] = 66 as i8
    b2 := mem.AllocateZeroed(8 as u64)
    mem.Copy(b2, b, 2 as u64)
    bytes2 := b2 as i8*
    println bytes2[0], bytes2[1], bytes2[2]
    mem.MemMove(b, (b as i64 + 1) as void*, 1 as u64)
    println bytes[0]
    b3 := mem.Reallocate(b, 64 as u64)
    arr := mem.AllocateArray(4 as u64, 8 as u64)
    arr64 := arr as i64*
    println arr64[3]
    mem.Free(b3)
    mem.Free(b2)
    mem.Free(arr)
end
```

Output:

```text
65 66 0
66
0
```

# term

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/term/

Text colour and style, cursor movement, progress bars, reading keys and the mouse, and the terminal size.

The `term` package has everything a good looking command line program needs: text colour and style, progress bars, and for full screen programs, cursor movement and reading keys one at a time.

The colour functions, such as `Red`, return a new string and print nothing. When the output goes to a file or another program, or `NO_COLOR` is set, nothing is added and the text stays plain. `SetColorMode` changes that behaviour.

The functions whose names start with `Seq` only return the escape sequence, and the one with the same name without the prefix sends it right away. To read keys, put the terminal into raw mode with `MakeRaw` or `MakeCbreak`, and always put it back with `Restore`.

## Types

### `Bar`

```salam
struct Bar
```

A progress bar. Make one with `NewBar` and set the fields to change how it looks.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `total` | `int = 100` | The full value; 100 by default. |
| `current` | `int = 0` | The current value. |
| `width` | `int = 0` | The width of the bar in cells; zero means automatic, from the terminal width, between 8 and 80. |
| `label` | `str = ""` | The text that comes before the bar. |
| `fill` | `str = "#"` | The character of the filled part. |
| `head` | `str = ""` | The head character; when it is not empty it takes the last filled cell. |
| `empty` | `str = "-"` | The character of the empty part. |
| `color` | `int = 0` | The colour code of the filled part, such as `FgGreen`; zero means no colour. |
| `show_percent` | `bool = true` | Show the percentage; on by default. |
| `show_count` | `bool = false` | Show the count as `150/200`. |
| `show_eta` | `bool = false` | Show the estimated time remaining. |
| `hide_cursor` | `bool = true` | Hide the cursor while drawing; on by default. |
| `start_ms` | `i64 = 0` | The start time, used to work out the time remaining. |
| `drawn` | `bool = false` | Whether the bar has been drawn at least once. |
| `done` | `bool = false` | Whether the bar has finished. |

term-Bar.salam

```salam
import term

func main:
    term.SetColorMode(term.ColorNever)
    mut b := term.NewBar(200, "download")
    b.width = 20
    b.fill = "█"
    b.empty = "░"
    term.BarSet(b, 50)
    println term.BarRender(b)
    term.BarAdd(b, 100)
    b.show_count = true
    println term.BarRender(b)
    mut s := term.NewSpinner("working")
    defer term.SpinnerFree(s)
    println s.label, s.frames.len() > 0
    mut frames := Vector {} as Vector<str>
    frames.push("◐")
    frames.push("◓")
    mut s2 := term.NewSpinnerFrames("loading", frames)
    defer term.SpinnerFree(s2)
    repeat 3:
        println term.SpinnerFrame(s2)
        s2.idx = (s2.idx + 1) % frames.len()
    end
end
```

Output:

```text
download [█████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░]  25%
download [███████████████░░░░░]  75% 150/200
working true
◐
◓
◐
```

### `Spinner`

```salam
struct Spinner
```

A spinner: a "working on it" sign for work whose progress is not known.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frames` | `Vector` | The frames of the spinner, shown in turn. |
| `idx` | `int = 0` | The index of the current frame. |
| `label` | `str = ""` | The text beside the spinner. |
| `color` | `int = 0` | The colour code of the frame; zero means no colour. |
| `drawn` | `bool = false` | Whether anything has been drawn on the screen. |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: term-Bar.salam

### `Key`

```salam
struct Key
```

One key that was read.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | `int = 0` | The kind of key; one of the `Key` constants. |
| `ch` | `str = ""` | The character, when the key is one. |
| `ctrl` | `bool = false` | Control was held as well. |
| `alt` | `bool = false` | Alt was held as well. |
| `shift` | `bool = false` | Shift was held as well. |
| `raw` | `str = ""` | The raw bytes that came from the terminal. |

term-Decode.salam

```salam
import term

func describe(k: term.Key): str:
    if k.code == term.KeyChar:
        ret "char " + k.ch + (k.ctrl ? " with ctrl" : "") + (k.alt ? " with alt" : "")
    else k.code == term.KeyUp:
        ret "up"
    else k.code == term.KeyEnter:
        ret "enter"
    else k.code == term.KeyEscape:
        ret "escape"
    else k.code >= term.KeyF1 and k.code < term.KeyF1 + 12:
        ret "f" + (k.code - term.KeyF1 + 1)
    end
    ret "code " + k.code
end

func main:
    each s in ["a", "\u001b[A", "\r", "\u001b", "\u0001", "\u001bx", "\u001bOQ", "\u001b[3~"]:
        println describe(term.Decode(s))
    end
    m := term.DecodeMouse("\u001b[<0;12;5M")
    println m.ok, m.button, m.col, m.row, m.pressed, m.motion
    println term.KeyDelete, term.KeyTab, term.KeyBackspace, term.KeySpace, term.KeyEOF, term.KeyUnknown
    println term.KeyDown, term.KeyRight, term.KeyLeft, term.KeyHome, term.KeyEnd, term.KeyPageUp, term.KeyPageDown, term.KeyInsert, term.KeyMouse, term.EscDelayMs
end
```

Output:

```text
char a
up
enter
escape
char a with ctrl
char x with alt
f2
code 19
true 0 12 5 true false
19 3 4 6 7 0
11 12 13 14 15 16 17 18 50 50
```

| `mode_out` | `int = 0` | The previous output mode on Windows. |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | Whether the mode change succeeded. |

term-ReadKey.salam

```salam
import term

func main:
    if not term.IsTTY(term.StdinFd):
        printerrln "this program has to run in a terminal"
        ret 1
    end
    mut state := term.MakeRaw(term.StdinFd)
    defer term.Restore(state)
    term.Write("press a key (q to quit)\r\n")
    until true:
        if not term.KeyReady(500):
            continue
        end
        k := term.ReadKey()
        if k.code == term.KeyChar and k.ch == "q":
            break
        end
        term.Write("code: " + k.code + "\r\n")
    end
    k2 := term.GetKey()
    b := term.ReadByte()
    password := term.ReadPassword("password: ")
    println k2.code, b, password.len()
    s2 := term.MakeCbreak(term.StdinFd)
    mut s3 := s2
    term.Restore(s3)
    ret 0
end
```

### `WinSize`

```salam
struct WinSize
```

The size of the terminal window.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cols` | `int = 80` | The number of columns. |
| `rows` | `int = 24` | The number of rows. |

term-Size.salam

```salam
import term

func main:
    w := term.Size()
    println w.cols > 0, w.rows > 0, term.Cols() > 0, term.Rows() > 0
    t := term.IsTerminal()
    println t == term.IsTTY(term.StdoutFd)
    println term.StdinFd, term.StdoutFd, term.StderrFd
    term.SetColorMode(term.ColorAlways)
    println term.SupportsColor()
    c256 := term.Supports256Color()
    ctrue := term.SupportsTrueColor()
    println c256 or not c256, ctrue or not ctrue
end
```

Output:

```text
true true true true
true
0 1 2
true
true true
```

## Constants and variables

### `Reset`

```salam
const Reset: str = "[0m"
```

The sequence that removes every colour and style.

term-Color.salam

```salam
import term
import str

func show(s: str): str:
    ret str.Replace(s, term.Esc, "\\e")
end

func main:
    term.SetColorMode(term.ColorAlways)
    println show(term.Red("error")), show(term.Green("ok")), show(term.Yellow("warning"))
    println show(term.Bold("important")), show(term.Underline("link")), show(term.Italic("quote"))
    println show(term.Dim("a")), show(term.Blink("b")), show(term.Inverse("c")), show(term.Hidden("d")), show(term.Strike("e"))
    println show(term.Black("a")), show(term.Blue("b")), show(term.Magenta("c")), show(term.Cyan("d")), show(term.White("e")), show(term.Gray("f"))
    println show(term.BrightRed("a")), show(term.BrightGreen("b")), show(term.BrightYellow("c")), show(term.BrightBlue("d")), show(term.BrightMagenta("e")), show(term.BrightCyan("f")), show(term.BrightWhite("g"))
    println show(term.OnRed("a")), show(term.OnGreen("b")), show(term.OnYellow("c")), show(term.OnBlue("d")), show(term.OnMagenta("e")), show(term.OnCyan("f")), show(term.OnWhite("g"))
    println show(term.Color256("orange", 208)), show(term.OnColor256("x", 236))
    println show(term.RGB("hello", 255, 92, 0)), show(term.OnRGB("x", 10, 10, 10))
    println show(term.Style("x", term.StyleBold)), show(term.Paint("x", term.Sgr(term.FgRed)))
    println show(term.SeqFg256(208)), show(term.SeqBg256(17)), show(term.SeqFgRGB(1, 2, 3)), show(term.SeqBgRGB(4, 5, 6))
    println show(term.Reset), show(term.Csi)
    term.SetColorMode(term.ColorNever)
    println term.Red("no colour"), term.ColorMode() == term.ColorNever, term.ColorAuto
end
```

Output:

```text

\e[41ma\e[0m \e[42mb\e[0m \e[43mc\e[0m \e[44md\e[0m \e[45me\e[0m \e[46mf\e[0m \e[47mg\e[0m
```

## Functions

### `SeqUp`

```salam
func SeqUp(n: int): str
```

The sequence that moves the cursor `n` rows up.

term-Seq.salam

```salam
import term
import str

func show(s: str): str:
    ret str.Replace(str.Replace(s, term.Esc, "\\e"), "\u0007", "\\a")
end

func main:
    println show(term.SeqUp(2)), show(term.SeqDown(1)), show(term.SeqRight(3)), show(term.SeqLeft(3))
    println show(term.SeqNextLine(1)), show(term.SeqPrevLine(1)), show(term.SeqColumn(10)), show(term.SeqMoveTo(5, 20)), show(term.SeqHome())
    println show(term.SeqSaveCursor()), show(term.SeqRestoreCursor()), show(term.SeqHideCursor()), show(term.SeqShowCursor())
    println show(term.SeqClearScreen()), show(term.SeqClearScrollback()), show(term.SeqClearLine())
    println show(term.SeqClearToLineEnd()), show(term.SeqClearToLineStart()), show(term.SeqClearBelow()), show(term.SeqClearAbove()), show(term.SeqResetLine())
    println show(term.SeqScrollUp(2)), show(term.SeqScrollDown(2)), show(term.SeqInsertLines(1)), show(term.SeqDeleteLines(1))
    println show(term.SeqScrollRegion(2, 20)), show(term.SeqResetScrollRegion())
    println show(term.SeqEnterAltScreen()), show(term.SeqExitAltScreen())
    println show(term.SeqEnableMouse()), show(term.SeqEnableMouseMotion()), show(term.SeqDisableMouse())
    println show(term.SeqTitle("my program"))
end
```

Output:

```text
\e[2A \e[1B \e[3C \e[3D
\e[1E \e[1F \e[10G \e[5;20H \e[H
\e7 \e8 \e[?25l \e[?25h
\e[2J\e[H \e[3J \e[2K
\e[K \e[1K \e[J \e[1J \e[2K
\e[2S \e[2T \e[1L \e[1M
\e[2;20r \e[r
\e[?1049h \e[?1049l
\e[?1000h\e[?1006h \e[?1003h\e[?1006h \e[?1006l\e[?1003l\e[?1002l\e[?1000l
\e]0;my program\a
```

### `Up`

```salam
func Up(n: int)
```

Moves the cursor `n` rows up.

term-Screen.salam

```salam
import term

func main:
    term.EnableAnsi()
    term.SetTitle("dashboard")
    term.EnterAltScreen()
    term.HideCursor()
    term.ClearScreen()
    term.Home()
    term.MoveTo(2, 4)
    term.Write(term.Bold("hello from the dashboard"))
    term.SaveCursor()
    term.Down(2)
    term.Right(4)
    term.Emit("status: good")
    term.RestoreCursor()
    term.Up(1)
    term.Left(1)
    term.NextLine(1)
    term.PrevLine(1)
    term.Column(1)
    term.ClearLine()
    term.ClearToLineEnd()
    term.ClearBelow()
    term.ResetLine()
    term.SetScrollRegion(3, term.Rows() - 1)
    term.ScrollUp(1)
    term.ScrollDown(1)
    term.InsertLines(1)
    term.DeleteLines(1)
    term.ResetScrollRegion()
    term.EnableMouse()
    term.DisableMouse()
    term.Bell()
    term.Flush()
    term.ClearScrollback()
    term.ShowCursor()
    term.ExitAltScreen()
    term.WriteErr("done\n")
    w := term.Size()
    println w.cols, w.rows, term.Cols()
end
```

# time

https://salamlang.github.io/Salam/std/time/

The current time, durations, formatting and parsing dates, the monotonic clock, timers and tickers.

There are two kinds of "time" in this package. An instant is a number of seconds since the start of 1970 in UTC, the Unix epoch, and is what you use for dates and clock times. A duration is a span with nanosecond precision, such as "1 hour 30 minutes", which you can add up and compare.

Functions such as `Year` and `FormatDate` work in the machine's local time, and their `UTC` counterparts work in UTC. To measure how long a piece of code took, use the monotonic clock (`MonoNanos`) rather than `Now`; the system clock can jump forwards or backwards.

For the Persian and Hijri calendars and for time zones, see the calendar package.

## Types

### `DateTime`

```salam
struct DateTime
```

An instant, as seconds since the Unix epoch, the start of 1 January 1970 in UTC.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `epoch` | `i64 = 0` | The seconds since the Unix epoch. |

time-Local.salam

```salam
import time
import str

func main:
    t := time.FromLocalParts(2024, 3, 20, 9, 30, 0)
    println time.Year(t), time.Month(t), time.Day(t), time.Hour(t), time.Minute(t), time.Second(t)
    println time.Weekday(t), time.YearDay(t)
    println time.FormatDate(t), time.FormatTime(t)
    println time.Format(t)
    println time.FormatISO(t)
    r := time.FormatRFC3339(t)
    offset := time.LocalOffsetMinutesAt(t)
    println str.StartsWith(r, "2024-03-20T09:30:00"), (offset == 0) == str.EndsWith(r, "Z")
    dt := time.FromEpoch(t)
    println time.Epoch(dt) == t, dt.epoch == t
    println time.Epoch(time.NowDateTime()) >= t
end
```

Output:

```text
2024 3 20 9 30 0
3 80
2024-03-20 09:30:00
2024-03-20 09:30:00
2024-03-20T09:30:00
true true
true true
true
```

### `Duration`

```salam
struct Duration
```

A span of time with nanosecond precision; it may be negative.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ns` | `i64 = 0` | The span in nanoseconds. |

time-Duration.salam

```salam
import time

func main:
    d := time.Hours(1).add(time.Minutes(30))
    println d.to_str(), d.minutes(), d.secs()
    println time.FormatDuration(time.Milliseconds(1500)), time.FormatDuration(time.Microseconds(250)), time.FormatDuration(time.Nanoseconds(42))
    println time.Seconds(90).to_str(), time.Days(2).hours(), time.SecondsF(0.25).millis()
    p := time.ParseDuration("1h15m30.5s")
    println p.ok, p.value.to_str(), p.value.seconds()
    println time.ParseDuration("ten minutes").ok, time.ParseDurationOr("?", time.Seconds(5)).to_str()
    k := time.Minutes(7)
    println k.sub(time.Minutes(10)).to_str(), k.neg().abs().to_str(), k.neg().is_negative()
    println k.mul(3).to_str(), k.div(2).to_str(), time.Hours(1).ratio(k)
    println k.cmp(time.Seconds(420)), k.less(time.Hours(1)), k.equals(time.Seconds(420))
    t := time.Milliseconds(1750)
    println t.truncate(time.Seconds(1)).to_str(), t.round(time.Seconds(1)).to_str()
    println t.nanos(), t.micros(), t.millis(), time.ZeroDuration().is_zero(), t.days() < 0.001
end
```

Output:

```text
1h30m0s 90 5400
1.5s 250us 42ns
1m30s 48 250
true 1h15m30.5s 4530.5
false 5s
-3m0s 7m0s true
21m0s 3m30s 8
0 true true
1s 2s
1750000000 1750000 1750 true true
```

### `DurationResult`

```salam
struct DurationResult
```

The result of parsing a duration.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |

The example for this item is shown with the ones above: time-Duration.salam

### `TimeResult`

```salam
struct TimeResult
```

The result of parsing a date and time.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ok` | `bool = false` | Whether the text was read successfully. |
| `epoch` | `i64 = 0` | The instant that was read, in seconds since the Unix epoch. |
| `nanos` | `int = 0` | The fraction of a second, in nanoseconds. |

time-UTC.salam

```salam
import time

func main:
    t := time.FromUTCParts(2024, 3, 20, 14, 5, 9)
    println t, time.FormatISOUTC(t)
    println time.YearUTC(t), time.MonthUTC(t), time.DayUTC(t), time.HourUTC(t), time.MinuteUTC(t), time.SecondUTC(t)
    println time.FormatHTTPDate(t)
    println time.ParseHTTPDate("Wed, 20 Mar 2024 14:05:09 GMT").epoch == t
    p := time.ParseISO("2024-03-20T17:35:09+03:30")
    println p.ok, p.epoch == t, p.nanos
    println time.ParseISOIn("2024-03-20 17:35:09.25", 210).epoch == t, time.ParseISOIn("2024-03-20 17:35:09.25", 210).nanos
    f := time.ParseFormat("%d/%m/%Y %H:%M %z", "20/03/2024 14:05 +0000")
    println f.ok, time.FormatISOUTC(f.epoch)
    println time.ParseISO("tomorrow").ok, time.ParseISOOr("tomorrow", 0)
    later := time.AddDuration(t, time.Days(10))
    println time.FormatISOUTC(later), time.DiffSeconds(later, t), time.DurationBetween(later, t).to_str()
    println time.SecondsPerMinute, time.SecondsPerHour, time.SecondsPerDay
end
```

Output:

```text
1710943509 2024-03-20T14:05:09Z
2024 3 20 14 5 9
Wed, 20 Mar 2024 14:05:09 GMT
true
true true 0
true 250000000
true 2024-03-20T14:05:00Z
false 0
2024-03-30T14:05:09Z 864000 240h0m0s
60 3600 86400
```

### `Timer`

```salam
struct Timer
```

A one-shot timer: it says whether the span you set has passed.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `deadline_ns` | `i64 = 0` | The end instant on the monotonic clock, in nanoseconds. |
| `active` | `bool = false` | Whether the timer is running. |

time-Timer.salam

```salam
import time

mut count := 0

func main:
    mut timer := time.NewTimer(time.Milliseconds(100))
    println timer.expired(), timer.remaining().millis() > 0
    timer.wait()
    println timer.expired(), timer.remaining().is_zero()
    timer.reset(time.Seconds(10))
    timer.stop()
    println timer.expired(), timer.active
    mut ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Milliseconds(50))
    println ticker.fired()
    ticker.wait()
    time.Sleep(120)
    println ticker.fired(), ticker.dropped >= 1
    ticker.advance()
    println ticker.remaining().millis() <= 100
    ticker.reset(time.Milliseconds(5))
    ticker.stop()
    println ticker.fired()
    time.AfterFunc(time.Milliseconds(10), (): println "after 10 milliseconds" end)
    time.RepeatEvery(time.Milliseconds(5), 2, (): println "tick" end)
    println time.Every(time.Milliseconds(5), (): count += 1 ret count < 3 end)
    count = 0
    println time.WaitUntil((): count += 1 ret count >= 3 end, time.Milliseconds(5), time.Seconds(5))
    println time.WaitUntil((): ret false end, time.Milliseconds(5), time.Milliseconds(20))
end
```

Output:

```text
false true
true true
false false
false
true true
true
false
after 10 milliseconds
tick
tick
3
true
false
```

### `Ticker`

A ticker: it "ticks" at a fixed interval.

| Name | Type | Description |

```salam
import time

func main:
    start := time.Now()
    a := time.MonoNanos()
    time.Sleep(20)
    time.SleepFor(time.Milliseconds(10))
    b := time.MonoNanos()
    println time.ElapsedMs(a, b) >= 30.0, time.ElapsedUs(a, b) >= 30000.0, time.ElapsedSec(a, b) < 5.0
    println time.SinceNanos(a) >= 30000000, time.SinceMs(a) >= 30.0, time.SinceUs(a) >= 30000.0, time.SinceSec(a) < 5.0
    println time.SinceDuration(a).millis() >= 30
    println time.MonoMillis() > 0, time.MonoMicros() > 0
    println time.Now() >= start, time.Since(start) >= 0, time.Until(start + 60) <= 60
    println time.NowMillis() / 1000 >= start, time.NowMicros() / 1000000 >= start, time.NowNanos() / 1000000000 >= start
end
```

```text
true
```
